cur:catacombs-two-brothers-sarcophagus.summary: A shell medallion with two male portraits divides two dense registers of biblical scenes: Christ raising Lazarus, multiplying the loaves and healing the blind, Peter's denial and arrest, Daniel among the lions and Abraham's sacrifice. Its deep carving and crowded, lively figures make it one of the finest double-register sarcophagi of Constantinian Rome.
facts: The name comes from the two male busts in the central shell, generally taken as brothers buried together.
Commons records its provenance as the 'cimitero di Lucina' and dates it about 325–350.

cur:manuscripts-girona-beatus-lamb-sea-o.summary: Above, seven angels with the last plagues stand in a row against a dark sky; below, the Lamb, labelled 'Agnus', with a cross-nimbus, stands on a mound before a blue medallion, while the victorious saints holding harps (citharae) sing on either side above a dark sea of glass. The scene illustrates the 'song of Moses and of the Lamb'.
facts: With 184 surviving miniatures on 284 leaves, it is described as one of the most richly decorated and best documented of the Beatus commentaries.

The Girona Beatus was completed on 6 July 975 for an abbot Dominicus, probably at the monastery of Tábara; unusually, its painters are named: 'Ende, woman painter and servant of God', and the monk-priest Emeterius.
cur:manuscripts-girona-beatus-lamb-sea-o.notes: Christ appears as the Lamb. Folio not given on the Commons file.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-33-christ.summary: At the upper right the Christ-Logos stands in a mandorla among angels and hands a sword to an angel flying up to receive it, 'the angel of the Lord encampeth round about them that fear him'. Rays from the mandorla fall on the psalmist's company and on three martyrdoms below — Peter crucified head downward, Paul beheaded and Lawrence on the gridiron — each with an angel to receive the soul. The artist reads the psalm as a promise to the martyrs.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
After centuries in England the manuscript arrived in Utrecht in 1716; it is often called the most valuable manuscript in the Netherlands.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-33-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:monumental-santa-prassede-zeno-porta.summary: This medallion from the inner arc of the San Zeno portal shows the Virgin in a dark maphorion holding before her breast a small medallion-like bust of the Christ Child, against a field of gold tesserae. Simply drawn with bold outlines, it echoes the Byzantine icon type of the Virgin presenting her Son.
facts: The Chapel of Saint Zeno was built by Pope Paschal I (817–824) as a funerary chapel for his mother, Theodora; its walls and vault are almost entirely clad in gold-ground mosaic.
The Virgin and Child crown the inner arc of medallions over the chapel door, with Christ himself at the top of the outer arc.

cur:monumental-tokali-jairus-daughter.summary: Inside a house indicated by columns and arches, the girl lies on a bed covered with a richly patterned red cloth, while the haloed Christ at the head of the bed raises his hand over her; apostles and her family stand around. The scene belongs to the extensive cycle of Christ's miracles painted in the church.
facts: Tokalı Kilise ('Church of the Buckle'), the largest church at Göreme, comprises an Old Church of the 10th century, painted in strips of red and green, and a larger New Church of the late 10th or early 11th century whose walls are dominated by rich indigo blue made from lapis lazuli.

Wikipedia notes that the lapis lazuli used in the New Church alone has been estimated as worth some 31.5 pounds of gold; the donors are often thought to have been the Phokas family, though without firm evidence.

cur:monumental-tokali-jairus-daughter.notes: The photograph shows a detail of the wall; whether the scene belongs to the Old or the New Church is not stated in the source. Dates for both phases are debated (c. 910s–920s for the Old Church; mid-10th to early 11th century for the New).

feat:faras-cathedral-nativity.summary: The Virgin Mary reclines on a great couch in the centre, while the swaddled Christ child lies in the manger beside her, surrounded by angels, shepherds and the Magi riding on horseback. Painted on a wall of the cathedral of Faras, on the Nile in what is now northern Sudan, it is one of the great masterpieces of Christian Nubian art. Its bold colours and serene, large-eyed faces bear witness to a flourishing African Christian kingdom that endured for nearly a thousand years.
facts: The cathedral had been buried by desert sand for centuries and was excavated by a Polish expedition led by Kazimierz Michałowski in 1960–1964, just before the rising waters of Lake Nasser flooded the site.
More than a hundred wall paintings were rescued and divided between the National Museum of Sudan in Khartoum and the National Museum in Warsaw.
The Nubian kingdoms converted to Christianity in the mid-sixth century through missions sent from Constantinople.
Nubian painters adapted Byzantine iconography but developed their own style, with distinctive facial types and rich ornamental dress.

Q3504778.summary: Judas wraps Christ in his billowing yellow cloak and leans in for the kiss, and the two profiles meet eye to eye — betrayal answered by a calm, piercing gaze. Around them torches, clubs and lances bristle against the blue night, while at the left Peter slashes at the ear of the high priest's servant. Few images in Western art concentrate so much drama into a single silent exchange of looks.
facts: Judas's cloak swallows Christ's body almost completely, so that only his head remains free — a visual metaphor of evil enveloping the innocent.

A hooded figure seen from behind, tugging at a fleeing disciple's robe, pulls the viewer into the crowd — Giotto likewise sets figures with their backs to us in the foreground of the Lamentation in the same chapel.
Yellow came to be associated with Judas in later medieval art, and Giotto's fresco is one of its most memorable uses.
